---
description: Give the interface a visual identity of its own, instead of the default look every generated app shares.
---

Everything in `.edgepoint/standard/ui.md` decides **how the interface is built and
how it behaves**. Nothing here overrides any of it.

This decides **what it looks like** — type, colour, spacing, motion, the one thing
a person remembers. The Standard is deliberately silent on that, and silence has a
default: every app built this way looks like every other app built this way, and
the builder can tell, even if they cannot say why.

## The line, before anything else

| | |
|---|---|
| **This governs** | the theme — typefaces, palette, scale, radius, density, motion |
| **`ui.md` governs** | shadcn/ui primitives, the three list states, forms, feedback, accessibility, responsive |
| **On any conflict** | `ui.md` wins. It is frozen; this is not |

So: **change the primitive once, never at the call site.** `ui.md` already says
this, and it is exactly the seam this works through — a distinctive look is a
theme applied to shadcn primitives, not hand-written buttons. If a design idea
requires bypassing a primitive, skipping an empty state, or dropping a focus
ring, the idea is wrong, not the Standard.

Accessibility is not an aesthetic axis. Contrast, focus visibility, semantic
elements and keyboard order hold whatever the direction. They are also how
Playwright finds things, so an inaccessible design is an untestable one.

## Ground it in the business

The builder told you what their business is. That is the brief, and it is a much
better one than most designers get.

A dental practice, a hardware store in Cebu, a tutoring service, a
church-supplies wholesaler — each has its own materials, vocabulary, and
customers, and that is where a distinctive look comes from. Design for *that*
business, not for "a booking app". If the spec does not say enough, look at the
words the builder used in `spec.md`; they wrote them, and they are full of it.

## The default look to avoid

Generated interfaces cluster in a few places. Recognise them, then decide rather
than land there by gravity:

- warm cream background, high-contrast serif, terracotta accent
- near-black with one acid-green or vermilion accent
- indigo/violet gradient on white, `rounded-2xl`, soft shadow everywhere
- numbered eyebrows (01 / 02 / 03) on content that is not a sequence

Each is fine when chosen *for a reason this brief supplies*. None is fine as a
starting point. Where the builder has stated a direction, their words win
outright — including when they ask for one of these.

## Working method

Decide before building, in this order:

1. **Palette** — four to six named values, and where each is used. Derive them
   from the business, not from a Tailwind default.
2. **Type** — a display face with personality and a body face that stays readable
   at small sizes. Set the scale and weights deliberately. Type carries more of
   the identity than colour does.
3. **Density and shape** — spacing rhythm, corner radius, border weight. A
   dental practice and a hardware store should not share these.
4. **One signature element** — the single thing the page is remembered by. Spend
   the boldness here and keep everything around it quiet.

Then check the plan against the brief: if any part of it is what you would have
produced for any other business, change that part. Only then write code.

Motion is optional and easy to overdo. One orchestrated moment beats effects
scattered across the page, and `prefers-reduced-motion` is respected always.

## Two things specific to this framework

**The builder reads the copy, so write it as `ui.md` and the workflow prompts
would.** Name things by what a person controls, never by how the system is built.
Buttons say what happens — "Save changes", not "Submit" — and the name survives
into the confirmation. Empty and error states give direction rather than mood.

**Do not invent facts to fill a layout.** No placeholder testimonials, no
invented statistics, no logo strips of companies that are not customers. Ask for
real content, or mark a draft clearly. A plausible invention is a lie the builder
did not know they were telling — and on a marketing site it is the one they will
be judged on.

**Philippine context is part of the brief, not decoration.** Prices show as
`₱1,500.00`, dates as `11 Aug 2026`, and the layout is checked on a phone first
— most of these customers will never see the site on a desktop.

## A fuller version of this exists

Anthropic publishes a `frontend-design` skill with more depth on aesthetic
direction and self-critique. It is Apache-2.0 and worth adding:

```
npx skills add https://github.com/anthropics/skills --skill frontend-design
```

It installs to `.agents/skills/frontend-design/` and replaces this file. That is
the intended upgrade — edgepoint will not overwrite it, and `sync` leaves it
alone. What it does not know is this project's Standard, so the precedence table
at the top of this file still applies: `ui.md` wins.
